title: Renters Insurance Florida Hurricane Coverage: What’s Covered and What Isn’t
summary: Wind damage to your belongings is covered; storm surge and flooding are not. What renters policies pay after a hurricane, and the gap Floridians must close.
body_markdown:
## What's covered


Wind damage to your belongings


Furniture, electronics, and clothing damaged by hurricane winds or by rain entering through wind-damaged walls, windows, or the roof.


Somewhere to live


Loss-of-use coverage pays for a hotel and extra living costs if wind damage makes your apartment unlivable. Many policies also pay when officials block access to your street because of storm damage nearby, usually for up to two weeks.


Falling trees and debris


If a tree or windborne debris comes through a window and destroys what you own, that's a covered wind loss.


Spoiled food, in many policies


Some policies reimburse refrigerated food lost in a power outage caused by a covered storm — usually a few hundred dollars. Check yours before the season.


## What's not covered


Storm surge and flooding


Rising water is excluded from every standard renters policy, and storm surge causes much of the worst hurricane damage in coastal states. Contents-only flood coverage is sold separately through the NFIP and private insurers.


The building itself


The roof, walls, and windows are your landlord's problem — their policy, not yours.


Your car


A flooded or wind-damaged car is handled by the comprehensive portion of an auto policy, not renters insurance.


Water that seeps in slowly


Gradual leaks and long-term seepage are maintenance issues, not sudden storm losses.


## What hurricane exposure looks like in Florida


We track lease terms, FEMA flood zones, and NOAA storm history for thousands of Florida apartment communities. Two numbers stand out: severe wind is routine, and a meaningful share of renters are also in mapped flood zones — where the flood exclusion bites hardest.

## Check for a hurricane deductible


In Florida and other coastal states, many policies apply a separate — often higher — deductible to hurricane losses, triggered when a named storm is declared. It may be a flat amount or a percentage. Find the word "hurricane" or "windstorm" in your declarations page before the season starts, not after landfall.


## How to close the flood gap


A contents-only flood policy covers what renters actually own — no building coverage you don't need — and typically costs far less than the building policies homeowners buy. If your community is in a FEMA zone starting with A or V, treat it as part of the cost of the apartment. You can check any address on FEMA's flood map service for free.


Two more moves that cost nothing: photograph every room and receipts for anything expensive (an inventory turns a two-month claim into a two-week one), and confirm your loss-of-use limit — after a major storm, weeks in a hotel add up faster than most people expect.


## Common questions


Does renters insurance cover hurricane damage in Florida?


Yes, for wind. Florida renters policies cover belongings damaged by hurricane wind and wind-driven rain, and pay for temporary housing if the unit becomes unlivable. Storm surge and flooding are excluded — that requires a separate flood policy, which about one in five Florida apartment communities we track would be wise to price given their FEMA zone.


Does renters insurance cover storm surge?


No. Storm surge is rising water, and all flood damage is excluded from standard renters policies regardless of the storm that caused it. Contents-only flood coverage is available through the National Flood Insurance Program and private flood insurers.


Will renters insurance pay for a hotel during a hurricane evacuation?


Only in specific cases. If your apartment was damaged by wind, loss-of-use coverage applies. Many policies also include civil-authority coverage, which pays when officials prohibit access to your area because of storm damage nearby — typically limited to about two weeks. Evacuating ahead of a storm that never damages your area is generally not covered.


Do renters need flood insurance?


If you're in a FEMA high-risk zone (zones starting with A or V), yes — your renters policy will pay nothing for rising water. Contents-only flood policies for renters are among the cheapest flood products sold. In low-risk zones it's optional but often inexpensive.
